notes.meaning: The queen of Sheba traveled a very long way with a large caravan to see whether Solomon's fame was genuine. She asked him hard riddles and opened her mind to him, and Solomon answered every question with the wisdom God gave him. When we seek true wisdom, no effort or expense is wasted.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often note that the queen's visit was likely motivated by trade interests, since Solomon's expanding sea commerce threatened Sheba's ancient overland routes for frankincense and myrrh.

notes.meaning: The queen saw Solomon's palace, the rich food, the orderly way his servants were seated, and the fine clothes of his court. When she also witnessed his magnificent approach to the temple and his worship, she was completely overwhelmed with awe. Good order and reverent worship in a household bring great honor to God.

The queen confessed to the king that she had doubted the reports she heard back home. Having seen it all for herself, she realized that what she was told had not even captured half of his greatness. Real divine wisdom always exceeds what words can describe.

The queen declared that Solomon's officers and servants were deeply blessed because they were able to hear his wisdom every day. Being around wise and godly people is a great privilege that shapes our own lives.

The queen gave praise to the Lord for choosing Solomon and putting him on the throne. She recognized that God made him king out of His deep love for Israel, to lead the nation with fairness and justice.

differ.view: The queen's praise shows God's ancient promise to Abraham being fulfilled, as foreign nations began to encounter and bless the God of Israel.
Her words may have been polite royal courtesy rather than a genuine personal conversion to faith in Israel's God.

notes.meaning: The queen presented Solomon with a lavish gift of gold, rare gems, and an unprecedented amount of fragrant spices. When people value true wisdom, they are eager to show honor with generous gifts.

The trading fleets of King Hiram and Solomon brought valuable algum wood and jewels from Ophir. Solomon used this rare timber to build stairways for the temple and palace, and to craft fine instruments for the temple musicians.

Solomon granted the queen of Sheba everything she requested, outgiving what she had brought to him, before she returned home with her servants. This mutual giving shows royal hospitality and points to God's own overflowing generosity toward His people.
Solomon took in 666 talents of gold each year from his regular revenues. In addition to this sum, Arabian kings and regional governors brought him steady trade duties and tribute in silver and gold.

differ.view: The yearly sum of 666 talents of gold signals a subtle warning of spiritual decay, linking excessive wealth to human pride and the later beast of Revelation.

notes.meaning: Solomon used beaten gold to make two hundred large shields and three hundred smaller shields, placing them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. These dazzling golden shields served as royal ornaments of power and majesty rather than everyday armor for warfare.

Solomon constructed an unparalleled royal seat of carved ivory overlaid with fine gold. It featured six steps, an attached gold footstool, armrests flanked by lions, and twelve carved lions standing across the steps, symbolizing royal strength and the twelve tribes of Israel.
All of Solomon's drinking cups and the royal utensils in his hall were made of pure gold. Gold was so abundant in Jerusalem during his reign that silver was treated as having little value.

Solomon's merchant fleet sailed on three-year voyages in partnership with Hiram of Tyre. They returned carrying precious metals, ivory, apes, and peacocks, displaying the vast reach of Solomon's trade network.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars debate whether the ships sailed west toward Tartessus in Spain or south through the Red Sea to East Africa or Arabia, with 'ships of Tarshish' likely naming large, ocean-going vessels.

notes.meaning: Solomon surpassed all contemporary monarchs in both wealth and God-given wisdom. Kings from across the region sought his counsel and brought annual gifts of silver, gold, rich clothing, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.

Solomon maintained thousands of stalls for his chariots and twelve thousand cavalry, placing them in designated chariot cities and in Jerusalem. His peaceful rule stretched from the Euphrates River southwest to the border of Egypt.

Under Solomon, silver became as ordinary as roadside rocks in Jerusalem, and costly cedar wood became as plentiful as common sycamore trees. He also ran a large-scale import trade in horses from Egypt and other surrounding lands.

differ.view: Multiplying horses from Egypt was an explicit breach of Deuteronomy 17:16, warning readers of the quiet beginnings of Solomon's compromise.

notes.meaning: The full record of Solomon's reign was kept in the historical books of Nathan the prophet, Ahijah the Shilonite, and Iddo the seer. These prophetic writings served as authentic source records for the nation's sacred history.

Solomon ruled over all Israel in Jerusalem for forty years before dying and being buried in the City of David, and his son Rehoboam succeeded him. Death brings an end to earthly splendor, showing that the greatest human rulers must yield their crowns to God.

differ.view: The Chronicler's total silence about Solomon's late-life idolatry suggests that he repented before death and was pardoned by God.
The phrase 'rested with his fathers' is used of both wicked and godly kings, leaving Solomon's eternal standing uncertain after his tragic fall into idolatry.
